newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian cocoa processors hit by local prices.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian cocoa processors hit by local prices.

text.p: One of Nigeria's leading cocoa processing factories on Thursday said the industry was suffering from buyers willing to pay farmers over the odds for beans.

Femi Boyede, the export manager of the Stanmark factory, which processes about 13,000 tonnes of beans a year, said some buyers were looking for a way to get hard currency to export capital and could afford to pay more than processors.

"Nigeria's cocoa market appears to be the only one that does not obey the law of terminal prices," Boyede told Reuters in Lagos. "At a time when cocoa prices are falling at the terminal markets, they can be rising in Nigeria."
He complained that paying a local price of 115,000 naira ($1,405) per tonne in the main cocoa-growing areas for currently available mid-crop beans made it hard to be assured of a profit at export.

Stanmark is one of a few survivors of over a dozen cocoa processing factories in Nigeria, many of which were set up with borrowed money and which found that after they had paid for their equipment they no longer had the capital to buy beans to keep working through the year.
"We are the only one that does not shut down for lack of beans," said Boyede.
Part-owned by Cadbury's local unit, which produces chocolate drinks and other products, Stanmark also has an assured domestic market for powder, which other local processors can find hard to sell.

Crushing between 30 and 40 tonnes per day, Stanmark is operating at around 80 percent of its installed capacity, producing cocoa butter, liquor, cake and powder -- most of the derivatives destined for export.
Official figures from Nigeria's produce inspection agency show cumulative exports of cocoa butter reached 518 tonnes in May from the start of the year in October, against 833 tonnes the year before.
Over the same period cumulative exports of beans stood at 126,324 tonnes in May from 112,644 tonnes a year earlier.
Total exports for the 1995-96 (October-September) year reached 139,063 tonnes, according to official data.
Nigeria's cocoa bean exports have declined from above 300,000 tonnes per year in the early 1970s when attention turned to crude oil production.
Industry analysts say that unless ageing trees are replanted, harvests will decline still further in future.
